title: How are the mighty fallen (2 Samuel 1:17–27)
hook: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan

segments.voice: Yesterday, the medium at Endor set bread before a king who'd lost all his strength. Your line was she fed him. Did you feed someone who was low? Today, news reaches David from the battle. Day seven hundred forty-three.

Two objects are set down in front of David: a crown, and the band from a king's arm. The young man who brings them has come three days from the battle. Saul has fallen on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan has fallen with him. On paper, this is good news for David. The man who threw spears at him, who chased him through caves and deserts, is gone. The road to the throne is open. And David tears his own clothes. He and his men mourn and weep and fast until evening. Then David does something more. He makes a song.
screen: `SAUL AND JONATHAN, DEAD ON GILBOA.` → `THE ROAD TO THE THRONE IS OPEN.` → `DAVID TEARS HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: The text says David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan, and that it's written in the Book of Jashar. It opens with the beauty of Israel slain on the heights, and then the line it keeps coming back to: "How are the mighty fallen!" It isn't a statement. It's a cry. How. As if the mind can't make it fit. Then David says, don't tell it in Gath, don't announce it in the streets of Ashkelon, the Philistine cities, so their daughters won't rejoice. He curses the hills of Gilboa: no dew, no rain. And then the hardest part. He praises Saul. Saul and Jonathan, lovely and pleasant in their lives, not divided even in death, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who dressed you in scarlet and put gold on your clothing. Not a word about the spear. Not a word about the cave. David doesn't pretend Saul was good to him. He just chooses, for the length of a song, to grieve the king and not the enemy. Then the song narrows to one person. I'm distressed for you, my brother Jonathan. Your love to me was wonderful. And the refrain comes back, once more at the very end: how are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished. Some people are easy to grieve. Some aren't. This song holds both kinds at once, the friend and the man who hunted him, and it gives each of them honest tears.
screen: `WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF JASHAR.` · `TELL IT NOT IN GATH.` · `WEEP OVER SAUL.` · then, large: `HOW ARE THE MIGHTY FALLEN.` · then: `MY BROTHER JONATHAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grieve a complicated person. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who is gone, or gone from your life, and who was hard: a parent who hurt you, a boss, an ex, a friend who turned. You don't need to forgive them or excuse anything. Just look for one true thing worth mourning. Something they gave. A way they were strong. Who they might have been. Let it be sad, and let it be mixed. If you pray, you can hold David's cry: how are the mighty fallen. The bell holds the time.
lament. David's song over Saul and Jonathan, grieving the friend and the man who hunted him in the same breath. Today's word.
Your line: swifter than eagles. Today, say one good, true thing about someone who was hard to love. Out loud or on paper. Day seven hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Jews read David's lament in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; the refrain how are the mighty fallen comes three times in the song, in verses 19, 25 and 27.

fork.setup: you're David. the king who hunted you is dead, and his crown has been brought to you. what do you do?

fork.reveal: he mourns, fasts, and laments both of them, praising Saul as well as Jonathan: how are the mighty fallen.

original.note: Hebrew: how the mighty have fallen, the refrain of David's lament.

what a scholar hears: verse 18 says to teach Judah "the bow"; some readers take the bow as the lament's own name.
